sources.cite: AWS. CloudWatch Logs User Guide: Help protect sensitive log data with masking
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11: data protection policies 'audit and mask sensitive data that appears in log events ingested by the log groups'; matching data 'is masked at all egress points, including CloudWatch Logs Insights, metric filters, and subscription filters'; 'When you set a data protection policy, log events ingested to the log group before that time are not masked'; 'Only users who have the logs:Unmask IAM permission can view unmasked data'; findings emit LogEventsWithFindings in AWS/Logs.

sources.cite: AWS. CloudWatch Logs User Guide: Working with log groups and log streams
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11: 'By default, log data is stored in CloudWatch Logs indefinitely'; 'Any data older than the current retention setting is deleted. You can change the log retention for each log group at any time.'

sources.cite: HHS. Guidance Regarding Methods for De-identification of PHI under the HIPAA Privacy Rule
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11: PHI is individually identifiable health information, including demographic information, that relates to health or care and identifies the individual; the Safe Harbor identifiers include names, all elements of dates (except year) directly related to an individual such as birth date, email addresses, and health plan beneficiary numbers.

Read 2026-11-11: an impermissible use or disclosure is presumed a breach unless a risk assessment of four factors shows a low probability of compromise: the nature and extent of the PHI, the unauthorized person, 'Whether the protected health information was actually acquired or viewed', and the extent of mitigation; individual notice 'in no case later than 60 days following the discovery of a breach'. The scenario leaves that decision to the clinic's privacy officer, not the developer.

brief.situation: Monday 09:00. You are a developer for a chain of clinics' online booking app, a Lambda function behind API Gateway in us-east-2 (Ohio). While debugging, you notice the function's CloudWatch logs contain whole booking requests: patient names, dates of birth, insurance member IDs and the reason for the visit.
handover: The debug logging was added 14 months ago and never removed; about 2.1 million bookings since.
The clinics are a HIPAA covered entity. Their privacy officer decides whether something is a reportable breach.
The log analytics team set up a vendor feed for dashboards; you are not sure what it receives.
howItWorks: Learner-paced: nothing moves until you act. Investigate, stop the exposure, report, then run the next days.
The board shows where the logs go and who can read them; the meters show whether PHI is still being written and sent.
Before you run the next days you are asked what the data is and what you did. The debrief scores what you did.

phiQ.title: What is this data?
phiQ.context: In this booking app, which of the logged fields are protected health information?

choices.label: All of them together: name, birth date, email and member ID identify the patient, and the visit reason is their health information
choices.feedback: Right. Identifiers such as names, birth dates, emails and health plan numbers become PHI when tied to health or care information held by a covered entity; here they sit beside the reason for a visit.

choices.label: Only the reason for the visit; the rest is ordinary PII
choices.feedback: No. On their own they would be PII, but linked to a booking for care at a covered entity, the identifiers are part of the PHI.

then.log: Wednesday: the privacy officer cannot tell from what is left which records went where, and must treat all 14 months as affected.
Wednesday: the privacy officer starts the four-factor risk assessment with your report and the preserved logs.
Wednesday: the vendor's support team emails to ask why their dashboards show patient names. The privacy officer hears of it from them.
Thursday: still streaming to the vendor.

plan.question: Before you run the next days: what kind of data is this, where did it go, and what did you change and report?

parts.label: Identifying the data
parts.criteria: Classifies names, birth dates, emails and member IDs with the visit reason as PHI in a covered entity's booking app; names where it went (the vendor feed) and who could read it.
parts.modelAnswer: Names, dates of birth, emails and insurance member IDs tied to the reason for a clinic visit are PHI. They went to every engineer with log access and, through a subscription filter, to an outside vendor whose contract does not cover health data.

parts.label: Containment and reporting
parts.criteria: Stops PHI at the source (logging change) and stops the vendor feed; masks as defense in depth, noting old events stay unmasked; restricts readers; preserves evidence; reports to the privacy officer, who owns the breach assessment.
parts.modelAnswer: Change the code so it never logs bodies, remove the vendor feed, add a masking policy for anything that slips through, and limit readers and logs:Unmask. Keep a restricted copy so the privacy officer can assess what was exposed, then shorten retention. Report it the same day; whether it is a reportable breach is their call.

noProgress.rationale: The exposure was contained downstream but the code still writes PHI to logs: a miss, recovered, never target.

expertPath.text: Sample the fields: identifiers and visit reasons, so PHI. Trace destinations: a vendor subscription filter. Check readers: 40 engineers and a contractor.
Remove the vendor feed, deploy the logging fix, add a masking policy, limit readers and logs:Unmask.
Report to the privacy officer; preserve a restricted copy, then set retention to 30 days. The trade-off: keeping the old PHI a while longer, locked down, so the exposure can be assessed.

evidence.headline: The record was destroyed
evidence.body: Deleting the logs felt like cleaning up, but the privacy officer needs them to judge what was exposed and to whom. Lock them down and keep a copy; shorten retention after.

ongoing.headline: PHI kept flowing out all week
ongoing.body: The vendor feed, unmasked logs and the logging code each kept patient data leaving the account. Stopping any of them at once would have ended the exposure on Monday.

fixed.headline: Found, stopped and reported
fixed.body: You identified the data, found where it went, stopped it at the source and the exit, kept the evidence and reported it. That is the expert path.

partly.headline: Contained, by a rougher route
partly.body: Check whether you traced the destinations first, whether the code still logs bodies, whether the vendor feed is off, and whether the privacy officer was told.

time_up.headline: No decision
time_up.body: The logs keep filling with patient data.

scoring.modelReasoning: Identifiers such as names, dates of birth, emails and health plan member IDs, linked to the reason for a clinic visit, are PHI. Find where the logs go before changing anything: here a subscription filter sends every event to an outside vendor. Stop it at the source by logging only what operations needs (request ID, route, status, latency) and at the exit by removing the feed. A CloudWatch Logs data protection policy masks identifiers in new events at every egress point but leaves events already stored unmasked, so it is defense in depth, not the fix. Limit readers and logs:Unmask, preserve a restricted copy, and report to the privacy officer, who runs the breach risk assessment.
